Fatigue and depression in MS overlap on every questionnaire that tries to tell
them apart. Effort-based decision making offers a behavioural separation:
whether the cost of action or the value of the outcome is what has changed.

## Where the overlap comes from {.k-head}

Some of it is built into the instruments. Zaehle and Linnhoff compared two
versions of the same depression inventory in MS. The full Beck Depression
Inventory asks about tiredness, sleep and lost energy. Its fast-screen form
drops those items and keeps the mood ones, and on the shorter scale the
correlation with fatigue was weaker. So part of what looks like fatigue
predicting depression is one scale asking about tiredness and the other scale
asking about tiredness.

The instruments are not the whole story. Sparasci and colleagues brought in
objective measures alongside the questionnaires and the three still came out
tangled. In the FutureMS cohort of newly diagnosed patients, Chang and
colleagues mapped the symptoms as a network and found fatigue attached to
particular depressive items rather than to depression as a whole.

Some of the confusion is a word. Fatigue is what a person reports feeling.
Fatigability is the measurable drop in performance as a task goes on. Enoka and
colleagues make the case that the two track each other poorly, which means a
paper using one term for both will find overlaps it built itself.

None of that helps me in clinic. A patient tells me they cannot get through the
day. I do not know whether to write fatigue or depression, and after Enoka I am
not confident the patient and I mean the same thing by either word. Even if I
settle on fatigue, I still do not know what has changed to produce it.

## What effort-based decision making measures {.k-head}

Someone stops buying bread. Either bread got expensive or they stopped wanting
bread, and the fact that they stopped buying will not tell you which. Move the
price around and watch, though, and it will. Effort-based tasks do that: the
same choice is put to a person many times, a small reward for little work
against a larger reward for more, both amounts varied, and what comes out is the
exchange rate between them.

So "I cannot get started" gets two candidate answers rather than one. The reward
may have stopped being worth anything, which is what anhedonia describes. Or the
reward is intact and the action has become expensive. In clinic both of those
come out as the same sentence, and the task is the only place they separate.

Husain and Roiser made the case for reading apathy and anhedonia this way across
diagnoses instead of inside one, and the separation has since been shown in
patients. In Parkinson's disease, Le Heron and colleagues found apathy and
dopamine acting on effort-based choice through distinct routes. Saleh and
colleagues pulled apathy and depression apart on different parameters of the
same decision in small vessel cerebrovascular disease. Pooling the schizophrenia
studies gives a consistent reduction in willingness to work for reward, which is
what Blouzard and colleagues report.

## What has been tried in MS {.k-head}

Erani and colleagues came closest, and the result was null. Forty patients and
forty matched controls did a switching task with effort and reward varied
independently, rating their fatigue as they went. Effort raised reported
fatigue. Reward improved performance. The interaction between the two, which is
the thing the effort-reward account predicts, did not appear. Their own reading
is that the reward may not have been salient enough to produce it.

There is a second complication. Modelling two effort-based tasks, Müller and
colleagues found that willingness to work is not a fixed quantity: two hidden
states of fatigue build up on different timescales, one recoverable by rest and
one not, and both lower the value of effort. A single number for how
effort-averse someone is may be averaging over something that moves while you
measure it.

The paradigms are not interchangeable either. Bogdanov and colleagues went
through them and found that physical effort does not behave like cognitive
effort, that a choice made before exertion does not behave like the same choice
made after, and that it matters whether the demand is announced or has to be
learned. Which task you pick is part of what you find.

So the one attempt at this in MS came back null, and I would rather write that
than round it off. The question still looks worth asking to me. What would
settle it is a task that separates cost from value, run in patients whose
fatigue and depression have both been measured properly. Another questionnaire
will not do it. Data collection is running, and nothing is claimed here about
what it will show.
